topic_details.topic: Supreme Court rules DHS can terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians in 6–3 decision
narration: Maya: Let’s start with the big institutional shock from Thursday: the Supreme Court’s 6–3 ruling that DHS can terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians with almost no judicial review, in Mullin v. Doe and Trump v. Miot.

Ben: Yeah, this one’s huge. We’re talking about roughly 350,000 Haitians and about 4,000 to 6,000 Syrians who’ve been living and working here legally for years suddenly becoming deportable if the Trump administration chooses to move.

Maya: Statutorily, the majority leans on the TPS provision that bars "judicial review of any determination" by the DHS secretary on designation, termination, or extension. They read that very broadly, so courts basically can’t police how DHS exercises that power unless there’s a constitutional claim.

Ben: And the American Immigration Council points out the really chilling part: even if a decision to end TPS was openly unlawful under the statute’s procedures, courts still couldn’t touch it, because the majority says those aren’t reviewable questions at all.

Maya: Right, so from a separation‑of‑powers angle, this is a decisive win for the executive. DHS now has what amounts to plenary discretion over TPS designations and terminations, and Congress is the only real check—judges are effectively out of the loop unless the Constitution is directly implicated.

Ben: But there’s a narrative piece too: TPS was supposed to be temporary humanitarian protection tied to crises like earthquakes and civil wars. In practice, people build lives here over decades. This decision reframes all that as a pure policy lever an administration can yank with minimal accountability.

topic_details.topic: White House releases FY 2027 budget proposing deep cuts to non‑defense spending and ‘woke’ DEI programs
narration: Ben: Yeah, it’s like a split‑screen: one document saying "shrink government, kill the woke stuff," and another saying "jack up wages, reshape the labor market." They’re not just policy choices, they’re identity markers for each party.

Maya: Starting with the budget: the White House released its FY 2027 request earlier this spring, and it’s now driving the appropriations fight. Core move is a roughly **10% cut to non‑defense discretionary spending**, about $73 billion below 2026 levels.

Ben: And that 10% headline hides really brutal hits. Civilian agencies, especially science and environment, get hammered: EPA down by about **52%**, NSF by more than half, NIH down roughly **10.5%** with some institutes eliminated.

Maya: Budget analysts point out defense is the big winner: about **$1.5 trillion**, roughly a 40% jump over 2026. So this isn’t overall austerity; it’s a reallocation from domestic programs to military and some targeted tax policies.

Ben: And the rhetoric in the document matters: it talks about "slashing Green New Scam initiatives" and "rooting out woke DEI programs." That’s not subtle technocracy; it’s culture‑war branding baked into line items.

Maya: Substance‑wise, they highlight nearly **$2 trillion in projected savings** tied to the Working Families Tax Cut Act over the budget window. On paper, that’s their claim to deficit discipline: use tax reforms plus cuts to shrink the federal footprint.

topic_details.topic: Senate Democrats led by Chris Murphy unveil Living Wage for All Act to raise federal minimum wage to $25
narration: Maya: Let’s zoom out on the big domestic fight taking shape this week: Trump’s FY 2027 budget on one side, and Senate Democrats’ $25 minimum wage push on the other. Both are trying to define economic stakes heading into 2026.

Maya: Democrats on the Hill are already branding it as "America‑last"—arguing it hollowes out health, science, and education to fund a defense surge. They point to cuts across NIH, NOAA, NASA science and STEM engagement as directly undermining long‑term competitiveness.

Maya: Where this gets interesting is the clash with the other new marker Democrats laid down this week: Chris Murphy’s **Living Wage for All Act**, introduced in the Senate. That bill would raise the federal minimum wage to **$25 an hour** over five years.

Maya: Policy‑logic case from Democrats is straightforward: wage stagnation and inequality remain entrenched; a higher floor boosts purchasing power, reduces working poverty, and narrows racial and gender pay gaps—especially if tipped workers stop relying on sub‑minimum wages.

Ben: But this is also a symbolic stake in the ground. Everyone knows it faces "steep odds" in the current Congress and fierce opposition from business groups and Republicans. It’s defining the negotiating range ahead of 2026, not a bill that passes next week.

Maya: The mainstream economic defense cites research from high‑wage cities and states: modest minimum wage hikes have historically had limited effects on employment while significantly raising incomes at the bottom. Democrats are extrapolating that logic to a much higher target.

topic_details.topic: House Education and Workforce Chair Walberg introduces AWARE Act to track workplace use of AI
narration: Maya: Now overlay that with the third policy track that popped this week: how Washington deals with AI’s impact on workers. House Education and Workforce Chair Tim Walberg introduced the **AWARE Act**—the AI Workforce Assessment and Research Enhancement bill.

Ben: We’ve talked about OpenAI and AI chips all week; this is one of the first concrete moves to build a federal **data infrastructure** on AI in workplaces. It directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to collect and report how AI is being used and what it’s doing to jobs.

Ben: The pro‑AWARE case is almost technocratic: you can’t manage what you don’t measure. Without granular data, we’re flying blind on whether AI is mostly complementing workers, displacing them, or polarizing the labor market into high‑skill and precariat zones.

Maya: Business‑friendly conservatives tend to like the measurement angle—it’s not regulating models or banning tools; it’s informing policy. They’ll say this helps maintain U.S. competitiveness by aligning training and education with real‑world demand rather than hype.

Ben: Heterodox critics worry about the next step: once you have AI‑labor data, it becomes the justification for new regulation. Labor advocates will use it to demand guardrails; populists could use it to attack "job‑killing algorithms" even where there’s productivity gains.

Ben: And because this is Walberg, the bill lives inside the broader GOP frame: be skeptical of heavy AI regulation but open to studying workforce impacts, especially to protect U.S. competitiveness versus Europe’s more precautionary model.

topic_details.topic: House subcommittee holds ‘Workforce Rewired’ hearing on modern apprenticeships in the AI era
narration: Maya: That brings us to the related move on the Hill this week: the **“Workforce Rewired”** hearing held by the House Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Development, chaired by Burgess Owens. It focused on modern apprenticeships in an AI‑driven economy.

Ben: Lawmakers heard from witnesses about how apprenticeship and work‑based learning can become pathways into AI‑heavy sectors. Think advanced manufacturing, healthcare tech, logistics, not just coding bootcamps. This was pretty bipartisan—everyone agrees the old training model is creaking.

topic_details.topic: Euro zone core inflation unexpectedly ticks up, complicating ECB rate-cut path
narration: Maya: Let’s start with the vibe check from markets, because it’s a weird split-screen: on Friday the S&P 500 dropped almost 2%, the Nasdaq was off more than 4.5%, but the Dow actually finished up about 0.6%.

Ben: So, classic 2020s story: old‑school industrial-ish names in the Dow grinding higher while the shiny stuff bleeds. Nvidia down nearly 9%, Google off more than 8%, Palantir, Coinbase, Robinhood all getting smacked.

Maya: Exactly. It looks like a rotation out of the crowded AI/crypto trade into safer or at least more boring corners of the market. You see it in the VIX too – volatility up more than 6%, but not panic-level, more like a risk‑off reset.

Ben: And the macro backdrop kind of explains that mood: rates aren’t really giving anyone a break. The 10‑year Treasury is still around 4.37%, the dollar’s firming, and now Europe’s inflation is refusing to play along with the "soft landing and rate cuts for everyone" fantasy.

Maya: Right, let’s go there. On Friday, Eurostat’s flash data for June showed euro area headline inflation stuck at about 2.5% year‑on‑year, but core inflation actually ticked up to roughly 2.7% from 2.6% in May.

Ben: So even after the ECB finally cut rates once this month, the underlying price pressure isn’t gliding neatly back to 2%. Services are the culprit again – wages, hospitality, personal care, the stuff people actually feel.

topic_details.topic: U.S. consumer sentiment falls again as inflation worries persist
narration: Ben: And you can see the divergence in FX: the euro is weaker, trading around 1.14 dollars, which is a decent sell‑off on the day. That’s a world where U.S. assets still look like the higher‑growth, higher‑yield game in town.

Maya: What’s interesting is the asymmetry: Europe’s puzzle is wages and services; the U.S. puzzle is more about expectations and sentiment. We just got final June numbers from the University of Michigan survey, and sentiment fell again.

Maya: Put together, the euro‑zone inflation surprise and the U.S. sentiment slump give you a picture where central banks are very cautious about cutting, and households are very tired of the cost of living – not a great mix for risk assets.

Maya: Exactly. Some of Friday’s sell‑off is likely technical – positioning unwinds after a crowded long trade – but part of it is the same thing you see in the Michigan survey: a sense that consumers are pulling back, not accelerating.

Maya: Let’s connect this back to households. In the U.S., you’ve got core PCE inflation we talked about yesterday cooling to around 2.6% year‑on‑year, and now you layer on falling gasoline prices – that should help real disposable income slightly.

Maya: From a markets perspective, the big arc is divergence. The U.S. is creeping toward cuts later this year if the data cooperate; Europe has already cut once but might have to slow down. That gap shapes where global capital wants to live.

topic_details.topic: Oil prices rise for a third session on OPEC+ discipline and summer demand
narration: Maya: Now, let’s go back to oil, because this is where the macro story really twisted in the last 24 hours. Yesterday we flagged crude climbing for a third straight session, with Brent pushing above $88 and WTI near $84 on OPEC+ discipline and summer demand.
Maya: But by the time we’re looking at live prices now, the picture has flipped. Brent is down hard, trading around $72.60, and WTI is near $69.23 – we’re talking roughly 7% on the day in U.S. crude.

topic_details.topic: OpenAI delays public rollout of GPT‑5.6 as U.S. government seeks early access to frontier AI models
narration: Maya: On Friday, Reuters also reported that OpenAI is delaying the full public rollout of GPT-5.6 after the Trump administration asked for early access to the most capable frontier models before broad release. The reported framework gives federal reviewers a say over which customers get the preview first.

Maya: OpenAI’s been everywhere this week, but this is the governance chapter, not the hype chapter. The company’s GPT-5.6 doesn’t just arrive as a product; it arrives inside a new federal process for “covered frontier models,” with up to 30 days of early access for the government and selected trusted partners.

Ben: Benign framing, maybe, but the cynic’s version is obvious: once the state can delay a launch and help choose the first testers, the line between safety review and pre-clearance gets blurry fast. That matters most for cyber-capable models, because that’s where the policy anxiety is clearly concentrated.

Maya: Also on Friday, OpenAI launched Frontier, a new enterprise platform for building and managing work-focused AI agents with shared context, onboarding, feedback, and fine-grained permissions. The pitch is less “chatbot” and more “software employee,” at least for companies willing to let agents into workflows.

Ben: And there’s the tension: the product story says agents are ready to do real work, while the governance story says the most capable models still need human and government supervision before they’re unleashed. Those two narratives are colliding in real time, which is exactly why this feels like a platform shift, not just another feature drop.

topic_details.topic: New U.S. presidential order formalizes a voluntary early-access framework for covered frontier AI models
narration: Ben: That’s the real precedent: not formal licensing, but a soft gatekeeping system where the government gets a look under the hood before launch. The White House order this week even says NSA-led benchmarking will sort models by advanced cyber capability, which is a very national-security way to run AI policy.

topic_details.topic: Samsung plans record 1,000 trillion won investment in South Korea over 10 years with massive chip build‑out
narration: Maya: Back to the story we flagged yesterday: Samsung’s 10-year, 1,000 trillion won build-out is still the headline, and Reuters said the company is set to announce it on Monday in South Korea, with a possible 300 trillion won chunk for chip fabs in the southwest. This is industrial policy at truly staggering scale.

Ben: And the point isn’t just “Samsung spends big.” It’s that South Korea is trying to lock down semiconductor capacity the way countries used to lock down oil lanes. Yesterday’s version was a national mega-project; this week’s version is a state-backed bid to stay relevant in AI-era supply chains.

topic_details.topic: Noah Smith argues that a new American industrial policy is emerging around defense, green energy, and AI
narration: Maya: Let’s zoom out on the AI-and-industry discourse this week, because three big essays are quietly sketching a new map of power: Noah Smith on U.S. industrial policy, Tyler Cowen on Europe falling behind, and Ben Thompson on platform deals.
Ben: Yeah, this is one of those weeks where the think-piece layer is more important than the product announcements. It’s less “new model drop” and more “who actually runs the future economy?”

Maya: Start with Noah Smith. In his Noahpinion essay from earlier this week, he argues the U.S. is *already* running an industrial policy, even if nobody put a big “Five-Year Plan” label on it. The pillars are defense, green energy, chips, and AI.

Ben: And he makes it pretty stark. He says the main reasons for this policy “have nothing to do with ‘good factory jobs’…They’re about external threats — climate change and the military threat from China.” That’s a psychological reframe for voters.

Maya: Right. The slogan he cites is this is meant to be “a foreign policy for the middle class.” So things like the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act aren’t just domestic handouts; they are geopolitical tools that happen to create U.S. manufacturing.

Ben: But there’s also a vibe shift buried in that. For decades politicians sold trade and tech as consumer benefits: cheaper stuff, cooler gadgets. Noah’s saying: no, the selling point now is security plus dignity — safe climate, safe supply chains, respectable jobs.

topic_details.topic: Tyler Cowen highlights why Europe’s AI and tech ecosystem is falling behind the U.S. and China
narration: Maya: Now contrast that with Tyler Cowen’s Marginal Revolution post from this week on Europe. He basically says: Europe is structurally incapable of “winning” the AI race against the U.S. and China. Not just behind — structurally misaligned.

Maya: For Cowen, that’s the crux: frontier AI is so capital- and talent-intensive that it looks more like a military buildup than a normal tech market. Europe’s smaller markets, fiscal priorities, and risk-averse regulation just can’t match those burn rates.

Ben: From a cultural angle, that makes sense. Europe’s postwar identity is: regulate hard, protect social insurance, be skeptical of Silicon Valley-style disruption. Cowen’s saying that same identity now blocks them from ever writing Meta-sized checks for their own models.

Maya: Cowen also stresses how fragmented capital markets and a lack of large-scale risk capital push ambitious founders to the U.S. or UK. So even when Europe trains talent, the highest-upside projects migrate to ecosystems that can support 10- or 11-figure compute budgets.

Ben: True, but Cowen’s point is about bargaining power. If you don’t own at least one part of the frontier stack — hyperscale compute, or a top-tier model, or the key chips — you’re a price taker in the new industrial order. That’s a status hit for the EU project.

Ben: And that’s where Tyler’s Europe argument bites again. If you don’t have global-scale cloud platforms, you’re negotiating with companies whose margins depend on exactly the bundling Thompson describes. Your "regulate them" instinct runs into "we’re your strategic supplier."

topic_details.topic: Ben Thompson analyzes the latest big‑tech AI partnership and what it signals about platform power
narration: Maya: And this is where Ben Thompson’s Stratechery post from this week slots in. He analyzes the latest AI partnership between a major cloud provider and a frontier model company and basically says: the battle now is over distribution and defaults, not just model quality.

Ben: Yeah, he compares this to old browser and mobile OS bundling fights. Think Internet Explorer on Windows, or Safari on iPhone. The core question: whose model is the default inside the cloud you already use — and who captures the margin when you call that API?

Maya: He emphasizes that API pricing, inference costs, and integrated toolchains will shape developer choices more than leaderboard rankings. If your company already runs on a given cloud, and that cloud bundles a reasonable model at a discount, that’s hugely sticky.

Ben: Thompson’s line is essentially: these partnerships are less about having the objectively ‘best’ model and more about “strategic control over where and how AI features are surfaced to end users.” Whoever owns that junction owns the economic rents.

Maya: Thompson also draws on history: early bundling deals in browsers or mobile locked in user behavior for a decade. Inference layer bundling could do the same. Today’s default model in your office suite, CRM, or code editor might determine tomorrow’s market structure.

Ben: Status-wise, he’s describing the new patrons. If you’re a startup, your "lord" is whichever cloud’s credit program, API pricing, and integration gives you life. That’s less the romantic "open-source model" story and more a feudal map with Azure, AWS, and others as overlords.

topic_details.topic: A dominant pop album is sitting at No. 1 on Billboard and driving a fresh wave of TikTok dance and lip‑sync trends.
narration: Ben: Culture-wise, this week feels very classic: one absolutely dominant pop album that’s everywhere you go, and one little horror-comedy that’s turning into the “if you haven’t seen it yet, don’t talk to me” movie.

Maya: Yeah, it’s one of those weeks where the algorithms and the humans actually agree. Billboard’s 200 update that dropped earlier this week has Olivia Rodrigo sitting at No. 1 with *You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love*.

Ben: And that record is in full saturation mode now. You’ve got multiple tracks off it on the Hot 100, the album sitting at the top of the Billboard 200, and TikTok basically treating it like a choose-your-own-feelings-adventure soundtrack.

Maya: From the numbers side, it’s that sweet spot labels dream about: strong first weeks, but now really sticky streaming. The chart story is that it’s not just debut hype; it’s holding No. 1 while other big projects come and go.

Ben: And socially, it’s the first pop album in a bit that feels truly meme-native. Each song is basically its own micro-fandom: you’ve got the dance sound, the POV breakup sound, the “I am the villain in my own story” sound, and they all have different aesthetics.

Maya: You can see it in how TikTok is using it. The uptempo tracks are driving choreographed dances and transition edits, while the slower ones are getting the hyper-specific POV captions, like “POV: you’re romanticizing the worst week of your life while pretending you’re fine.”

topic_details.topic: A surprise viral horror‑comedy hit is dominating Letterboxd and group chats as the ‘you have to see this with a crowd’ movie.
narration: Maya: Yeah, this one is interesting because it didn’t open as a giant IP event. It’s a mid-budget original horror-comedy that came out in June, and over the last week it’s turned into a word-of-mouth hit, especially for Friday and Saturday night showings.

Maya: Critics are unusually aligned with the audience here. The reviews keep highlighting how it balances legitimately scary set-pieces with absurd humor, instead of undercutting every scare with a wink. It’s closer to *Get Out* than to pure parody.

Ben: It’s very reminiscent of how *Barbarian* grew. That same energy of, “Yeah, it starts as one thing, then the floor falls out from under you.” Except this time there’s more overt comedy baked in, so the laughter becomes part of the tension.

Maya: And from a business angle, it’s a good case study for mid-budget horror. You’ve got Deadline and others calling it a sleeper hit because, in a market dominated by superhero sequels and giant branded horror, this smallish, weird movie is carving out real box office via buzz.

topic_details.topic: Giannis Antetokounmpo being traded to Miami Heat in blockbuster deal
narration: Ben: Let’s start with the sports earthquake we flagged yesterday: the Giannis-to-Miami deal isn’t just rumor anymore, it’s being treated as structurally real by basically every NBA outlet, and the details, reported back on Monday, June 22, make it feel even more franchise-defining for both sides.

Maya: Yeah, the reporting across NBA.com, ESPN, and others now converges: it’s Giannis plus Bobby Portis to the Heat, with Milwaukee getting Tyler Herro, Kel’el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakučionis, and a stack of picks, including this year’s No. 13 and unprotected firsts in 2031 and 2033.

Ben: Narratively, that’s wild: you’re sending out essentially an entire young core and your future to graft a two-time MVP onto Jimmy and Bam. It turns "Heat Culture" from a gritty overachiever brand into a superteam project again, but with a very different profile than the LeBron-era spacing-and-playmaking model.

Maya: And from the systems angle, Milwaukee’s doing the exact opposite move: they’ve cashed out of the aging win-now core and turned Giannis into a diversified asset bundle—three firsts, a swap, plus four rotation-capable players. That’s a classic small-market hedge against the risk of an unhappy superstar on a mega deal.

Ben: There’s also the darker piece: with Portis in the deal and Thanasis a free agent, ESPN noted that there are now zero players left from the Bucks’ 2021 title roster. That’s not just a trade, that’s a memory wipe—one of the more abrupt endings to a championship era we’ve seen in the modern NBA.

Maya: And forward-looking, Giannis is reportedly extension-eligible in early January for up to four years and $275 million. So, structurally, this isn’t a rental. Miami is betting that it can lock in a post-prime but still dominant physical force and anchor its cap sheet around him deep into the 2030s.

topic_details.topic: Cape Verde becomes smallest-ever country to reach World Cup knockouts
narration: Maya: Let’s pivot from superteams to Cinderella stories, because the World Cup this week has produced one of the purest underdog arcs in years: Cape Verde punching into the round of 32, the smallest country ever to reach the knockout stage in the tournament’s expanded format.

Maya: FOX Sports and Reuters coverage over the past few days has stressed that point: Cape Verde didn’t fluke it with one wild upset, they managed their group with mature game states—closing out leads, surviving pressure, and showing an understanding of tournament tempo you usually associate with seasoned European sides.

Ben: And with the World Cup now expanded, they’ve become the test case for a big argument: does adding more teams dilute quality or widen the stage for genuinely competitive smaller nations? Cape Verde’s run is ammunition for the "competitive balance" side—it’s not Qatar-style host bump, it’s earned football legitimacy.

Maya: Structurally, you can already see knock-on effects. Scouting departments will start mining Lusophone Africa and the islands more aggressively, federations with similar profiles will push for investment, and Cape Verde’s youth generation just got a global proof-of-concept: this pathway isn’t fantasy anymore, it’s television reality.

Ben: So across the board this week, the sports stories rhyme: a superteam bet in Miami, a microstate rewriting World Cup hierarchy, a traditional power learning to win ugly, a host nation confronting its defensive demons, and a young WNBA big authoring perfection. Different leagues, same theme—power is getting redistributed.

topic_details.topic: Spain edges Uruguay to clinch World Cup knockout berth and win Group H
narration: Ben: And just as Cape Verde is rewriting the small-country script, Spain is quietly rewriting its own: from "beautiful but brittle" to something more like "gritty and relentless." On Friday and into Saturday recaps, they’re being framed as a team that keeps grinding out narrow wins, including edging Uruguay to win Group H.

Maya: USA TODAY lays it out: Spain needed a late goal to finally put away Uruguay and clinch both a round-of-32 berth and top spot in Group H. This is consistent with their group pattern—scorelines that don’t look flashy, but game control metrics and xG that say they’re dictating terms more than the final numbers suggest.

Ben: And that matters because Spain has lived for a decade under the shadow of tiki-taka nostalgia and "knockout disappointment." If they keep winning these stressful one-goal matches, the narrative flips from "can they play pretty" to "can they out-suffer everyone"—which is exactly what late-stage tournament football demands.

Maya: The bracket implications are real too. By taking Group H, Spain changes who lands in their half of the round of 32, potentially avoiding some early heavyweights and forcing others into more chaotic paths. Every late goal this week is essentially a bracket-editing event, and that Uruguay result re-seeded part of the tree.

topic_details.topic: USMNT loses first World Cup game but secures knockout clash with Bosnia and Herzegovina
narration: Maya: Back to the story we flagged yesterday with the home-soil twist: the USMNT’s 3–2 loss to Turkey in stoppage time on Thursday at SoFi still stings, but CBS and others now have the next chapter clearly set—Bosnia and Herzegovina in the knockouts next Wednesday, with the U.S. still coming in as a seeded group winner.

Ben: And that’s the weird emotional mix: you’ve just watched your defense collapse at the final kick in a game where rotation and complacency were obvious, but the reward is still a very winnable opponent in Bosnia, not a blue-blood. So fans are oscillating between "we’re fine" and "this back line is a liability."

Maya: CBS’s Kacey White and other analysts are basically issuing a checklist: restore defensive focus, sharpen set-piece marking, and be much less casual in build-up. The group stage let them learn those lessons in a low-cost environment; the problem is, emotionally, that Turkey loss felt high-cost in the national psyche.

Ben: The stakes for Wednesday are huge beyond just bracket position. This is a home World Cup; a round-of-32 exit to Bosnia would instantly reframe the cycle as a failure of growth, while a professional, controlled win could reset the vibe and turn the Turkey chaos into a "wake-up call" chapter in a deeper run.

Maya: From a systems view, Bosnia is a good test case. They tend to be structured, disciplined, and more reactive than proactive. If the U.S. can impose tempo, avoid cheap turnovers, and keep their flanks from being isolated, they should have the talent edge. If the sloppiness from Thursday repeats, it’s coin-flip territory.

Ben: Also, as we noted yesterday, tournament memory is sticky. Fans still remember 2010’s euphoric Landon Donovan winner; this cycle’s iconic moment so far is the opposite—a gut punch. What happens against Bosnia will decide whether the defining narrative becomes trauma or resilience in a World Cup they’re supposed to own.

topic_details.topic: Kamilla Cardoso sets WNBA record by going 13-for-13 from the field in 30-point performance
narration: Maya: Let’s close with a different kind of dominance story, this time in the WNBA. On Friday night, Chicago Sky center Kamilla Cardoso went 13-for-13 from the field, dropped 30 points, and set the league record for most field goals made in a game without a miss in a 124–94 win over the expansion Portland Fire.

Maya: AP emphasized that it’s a league record, not just a franchise one. In a WNBA that’s seeing an influx of size and skill at the forward and center spots, Cardoso posting a perfect 30 on an expansion opponent signals she can be the kind of interior hub you build around—finishing, offensive rebounding, and drawing extra attention.

Ben: Narratively, it also arrives right as the WNBA conversation is dominated by guards and wings—Caitlin Clark’s shooting, old-guard UConn alumni, the Liberty’s spacing machine. Cardoso’s record night is a reminder that, in this league, a terrifyingly efficient big can still tilt the geometry of the game in a single evening.

topic_details.topic: Supreme Court rules DHS can terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians in 6–3 decision
narration: Maya: Big picture today, it’s one of those whiplash Saturdays: a Supreme Court decision that could upend hundreds of thousands of lives, a budget and wage fight trying to define the 2026 economy, markets punishing the shiny stuff, and a 10‑year industrial bet from Samsung that feels almost sci‑fi in scale.

Ben: Yeah, it’s a day where institutions and narratives are doing most of the moving—Court, Congress, trillion‑won capex plans—while culture and sports give you that “the ground is shifting under your feet” feeling in a more human way: one album, one horror‑comedy, and, apparently, Giannis in South Beach.

Maya: Headliner first: on Thursday, the Supreme Court’s 6–3 rulings in Mullin v. Doe and Trump v. Miot basically said DHS can terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians with almost no judicial review, clearing the way for TPS to end for roughly 350,000 Haitians and 4,000–6,000 Syrians.

Ben: We’ll get into the legal mechanics later, but the headline is brutal: a program that’s been a quiet backbone of a lot of communities—people living and working here legally for years—can now be shut off as a policy choice, with courts largely on the sidelines except for narrow constitutional claims.

Maya: From there we’re zooming out to the domestic economic fight that crystallized this week: on one side, Trump’s FY 2027 budget blueprint, with its cuts to non‑defense spending and culture‑war line items; on the other, Senate Democrats floating a $25 federal minimum wage as their banner proposal.

Ben: It’s very split‑screen: one document saying “shrink government, kill the woke stuff,” another saying “jack up wages, reshape the labor market.” We’ll treat both as campaign manifestos as much as budgets—what they signal about who’s supposed to win and lose economically between now and 2026.
